title: Wealth as a trust
hookLine: wealth as a trust, with a right for the poor in it (51:19; 57:7)

lines: USE IT, DON'T SELL THE SOFA.
cards: A friend hands you a house key before a long trip. With it you can go in, water the plants, use the kitchen, even sleep there. But you'd never sell the sofa.

It isn't yours, and you both know it. You're holding it for someone, and one day you'll hand it back. One verse of the Qur'an talks about money in much the same way, and it has a word for the person holding it.

teach.b: Surah al-Hadid, verse seven, in Pickthall's translation, tells believers to "spend of that whereof He hath made you trustees." The Arabic word is mustakhlafin.

It comes from kh-l-f, the root of khalifah, a successor, someone who stands in for another. In this picture, a person holds wealth that someone held before and someone will hold after, and the owner is Allah.

teach.h: A KNOWN RIGHT FOR THE POOR.
teach.b: Surahs fifty-one and seventy add the second half: in the wealth of the righteous there's a right, a known right, for the one who asks and the one who is deprived. Not a favor. A right.

The money is held in trust, and part of it already belongs to someone else. Islamic law gives that part a shape in zakat: each year, a fixed share of savings above a set minimum goes to those in need.
Beyond it there's sadaqah, given freely, any time. A hadith in Sahih Muslim pictures the person who says, my wealth, my wealth.

teach.h: ATE IT, WORE IT, OR SENT IT AHEAD.
teach.b: The Prophet ﷺ said: what is yours of it is only what you ate and finished, wore and wore out, or gave away and so sent ahead. Everything else, you're leaving for others.
And another hadith in Muslim's collection: charity never decreased wealth. The trust doesn't get smaller when you hand part of it on. It's how the trust gets kept.

how: Muslims pay zakat each year, commonly 2.5 percent of savings held above a minimum (nisab) for a lunar year, and give voluntary charity (sadaqah) at any time; many reckon zakat during Ramadan.

o: the poor, who have a right to wealth
people who give their yearly zakat

games.q: wealth as a trust — tap the pairs.
p: a right for the one who asks

s: the Qur'an calls giving to the poor a favor
it calls it a right, a known right, in the wealth of the righteous.
a hadith says charity never decreased wealth
in the hadith, what you own is everything in your accounts
only what you ate, wore out, or gave away and sent ahead.

games.q: someone says: my wealth, my wealth. in the hadith, what does the Prophet say is truly theirs?
o: what they ate, wore out, or gave away.
whatever they leave to their children.
games.why: only what was used up or given away and sent ahead; the rest is left for others (Sahih Muslim).

practice: Picture what you own as if it were on loan: your money, your phone, your time, your skills, and hold the thought, I'm looking after this.
Then ask whose known right is in it: a relative who's struggling, a neighbor, a charity you trust, a coworker who needs an hour of your help.

wordCard.voice: Mustakhlafin. Trustees: in 57:7 wealth-holders stand in for Allah, the true owner, and in 51:19 the poor have a known right in what they hold. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 57:7: trustees, those made successors over it.

carryVoice: Your line: held in trust. Giving is returning, not losing. That's day six hundred eighty-two.

sources.q: spend of that whereof He hath made you trustees

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2588 (charity does not decrease wealth)
